reference.source: Postgraduate Haematology / Oxford Textbook of Medicine
clinicalPearls: A deficiency of coagulation factor XI from mutations in F11, inherited in an autosomal (not X-linked) manner and so affecting both sexes
It is notably more common in people of Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry than in the general population
Bleeding is typically milder and less predictable than in haemophilias A and B, and it correlates poorly with the measured factor XI level
Bleeding tends to be injury-related and is especially likely at sites of high fibrinolytic activity such as the mouth, nose and urinary tract, and after dental or surgical procedures
Spontaneous haemarthroses are uncommon, unlike in haemophilia A or B
The screening pattern is a prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time with a normal prothrombin time, and a specific factor XI assay confirms the diagnosis
Management is largely tailored to the bleeding history and procedure, using antifibrinolytics, factor XI replacement or plasma products, with individualised peri-operative planning
reference.pathophysiology: Haemophilia C results from mutations in F11 that reduce the activity of coagulation factor XI, a component of the intrinsic pathway that, once activated, amplifies thrombin generation partly through activation of factor IX. Its role is chiefly in reinforcing and sustaining the clot rather than initiating haemostasis, which explains why bleeding is usually milder and less consistent than with factor VIII or IX deficiency. Because factor XI contributes to protecting clots against fibrinolysis, bleeding is particularly prone to occur at sites rich in local fibrinolytic activity, and the poor correlation between factor level and bleeding suggests additional modifying haemostatic factors.
additionalDifferentials: Other contact-factor deficiencies (factor XII, prekallikrein) that prolong the aPTT without bleeding
Mild acquired coagulopathy or anticoagulant effect
additionalInvestigations: Activated partial thromboplastin time, prothrombin time and platelet count
Mixing study to distinguish deficiency from an inhibitor or lupus anticoagulant
Von Willebrand and platelet function testing where the picture is unclear
Bleeding history assessment to guide procedure planning
F11 genetic testing for confirmation and family or reproductive counselling
redFlags: Excessive bleeding after surgery or trauma at fibrinolytic-rich sites (oral, nasal, genitourinary)
Bleeding disproportionate to the measured factor level
Rare inhibitor development, particularly in severely deficient patients after replacement
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is generally good, with many patients only bleeding in response to surgery or trauma, and careful individualised peri-procedural management usually prevents serious bleeding.
pitfalls: Predicting bleeding risk from the factor XI level, which correlates poorly with clinical bleeding
Confusing an isolated prolonged aPTT with a non-bleeding contact-factor deficiency or a lupus anticoagulant
Over-transfusing plasma products and risking volume overload or unnecessary exposure
Failing to plan haemostatic cover before high-risk procedures at fibrinolytic sites
management: Reserve treatment for bleeding episodes and cover for surgery or trauma rather than giving routine prophylaxis, since bleeding correlates poorly with factor level
Use antifibrinolytics such as tranexamic acid as first-line cover for dental and other procedures at fibrinolytic-rich mucosal sites
For major surgery or significant bleeding, replace factor XI with factor XI concentrate or fresh frozen plasma, mindful of the thrombotic risk of concentrate
Individualise peri-procedural plans on the basis of personal and family bleeding history
Avoid antiplatelet drugs and NSAIDs where possible and inform surgeons and anaesthetists of the diagnosis before procedures
Manage through a haematologist with haemostasis expertise
Offer genetic counselling for this autosomal condition and screen relatives, noting increased frequency in those of Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry
